translationRepairs: Lady of the District Qu bore the Prince of Hengyang, Jun;
Honorable Lady Qu bore the Prince of Hengyang, Jun;
區貴人 is surname Qu plus the inner-palace rank 貴人; neighboring consorts are likewise named by rank (修容, 太妃, 淑妃, 美人), not as a lady of a district.
Prince Xian of Linchuan, Ying, styled Xuangguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
Prince Xian of Linchuan, Ying, styled Xuanguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
字宣光 is the courtesy name Xuanguang; Xuangguang is a misspelling.
Prince Xian of Linchuan Ying, styled Xuangguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
Prince Xian of Linchuan Ying, styled Xuanguang, was the founding emperor's third son.
The same courtesy name 宣光 must be Xuanguang in the literal field as well.

When the affair was settled, he was made adviser to the central army, attendant gentleman, aide to the state, general of assisting the state, and grand administrator of Huainan and Xuancheng — both posts he declined.

When the affair was settled, he was made adviser to the central army, attendant gentleman, general of assisting the state, and grand administrator of Huainan and Xuancheng — none of which he accepted.
並不拜 covers every listed appointment, and 輔國將軍 is a single title, not an extra 'aide to the state'; the proposed list still inserts a superfluous 'and' before that generalship.
In year five he was made Grand Mentor with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes at his present rank.
In year five, at his present rank, he was granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
即本號開府儀同三司 is the privilege of opening a headquarters with Three-Dukes ceremony at his existing rank, not appointment as Grand Mentor (太傅).
In year five he was made Grand Mentor with the same title at his present rank.
In year five, at his present rank, he was granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
The literal field likewise misrenders 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor; 即本號 keeps his present title while granting that privilege.
The emperor was furious and by his own hand issued an edict a beating with the staff.
The emperor was furious and by his own hand issued an edict ordering a beating with the staff.
手詔賜杖 is an imperial handwritten edict ordering a staff beating; the original English is ungrammatical and drops the verb of command.
The emperor was greatly angered and by hand-edict granted him a beating staff.
The emperor was greatly angered and by handwritten edict granted him a beating with the staff.
賜杖 is punishment by beating with the staff, not the conferral of a staff as an object.
Contemporaries judged Emperor Wu better than Cao Pi and less than Liu Zhuang of Han Ming.
Contemporaries judged Emperor Wu better than Emperor Wen of Wei and less than Emperor Ming of Han.
The Chinese compares 世祖 with 魏文 and 漢明, the posthumous titles of Wei Wendi and Han Mingdi; 'Cao Pi' and 'Liu Zhuang of Han Ming' invent personal names and garble 漢明.
At his present rank he was posthumously made Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony.
At his present rank he was posthumously granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
贈開府儀同三司 is a posthumous grant of headquarters with Three-Dukes ceremony, not Grand Mentor.
At his present rank he was posthumously made Grand Mentor with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes.
At his present rank he was posthumously granted a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes.
The literal field repeats the same false Grand Mentor rendering of 開府儀同三司.
The founding emperor often said: "This is our house's Prince of Ren."
The founding emperor often said: "This is our house's Prince of Rencheng."
任城 is the fief Rencheng; 'Prince of Ren' truncates the place-name in 此我家任城也.
The founding emperor often said: "This is my family's Prince of Ren."
The founding emperor often said: "This is my family's Prince of Rencheng."
The literal quotation likewise needs the full fief name Rencheng for 任城.
When Emperor Wu ascended Ye was advanced to General of the Left and entered as director of the secretariat, rank unchanged.
When Emperor Wu ascended, Ye was advanced to General of the Left and entered as director of the secretariat, rank unchanged.
世祖即位，進號… has a clause break after the accession; without the comma, 'ascended Ye' garden-paths Ye as the object of accession.
Soon he was transferred former general and grand minister of rituals, repeatedly thwarted in his aims.
Soon he was transferred to Front General and grand minister of rituals, repeatedly thwarted in his aims.
前將軍 is the office Front General, not a 'former' general.
On his deathbed the Shizu's final edict made Ye Defender General and Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony, with martial pipes and drums.
On his deathbed the Shizu's final edict made Ye General of the Guards and granted him a headquarters with ceremonial equality to the Three Dukes, with martial pipes and drums.
衛將軍 is General of the Guards, not Defender General (護軍), and 開府儀同三司 is not Grand Mentor; the proposed 'an office with ceremonial equal' is still awkward.
In year four he went out bearer of credentials, commander of Jinxu affairs in Jiang and Yu, Southern Central Army General, and governor of Jiang.
In year four he went out bearer of credentials, commander of Jinxi affairs in Jiang and Yu, Southern Central Army General, and governor of Jiang.
晉熙 is Jinxi; Jinxu is a corrupted romanization.
In Yanxing year one he was posthumously advanced to Grand Mentor, attendant and Rapid Cavalry unchanged.
In Yanxing year one he was advanced to Minister of Education, with attendant and Rapid Cavalry unchanged.
進位司徒 is a living advancement to Situ (Minister of Education); the text has neither 追/贈 nor 太傅, and the following narrative still shows him alive.
In the first year of Yanxing he was posthumously advanced to Grand Mentor, attendant and Rapid Cavalry as before.
In the first year of Yanxing he was advanced to Minister of Education, with attendant and Rapid Cavalry as before.
The literal field makes the same two errors: there is no posthumous marker, and 司徒 is not Grand Mentor.
When the Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was made general of the central army and Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony.
When the Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was made General of the Central Army and granted open office with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes.
鑠遷中軍將軍，開府儀同三司 grants central-army generalship plus the Three-Dukes ceremonial privilege, not Grand Mentor.
When Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was moved general of the central army and Grand Mentor with Three-Dukes ceremony.
When Prince of Poyang was killed, Shuo was moved General of the Central Army and granted open office with ceremony equal to the Three Dukes.
The literal field likewise misidentifies 開府儀同三司 as Grand Mentor.
He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the fief moved to Suizhou and the title changed.
He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the fief's name followed the commandery's change of name.
后國隨郡改名 means the princely title followed the commandery's rename (廣興 to 始興), not a transfer to Suizhou.
He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the state followed Suizhou and the name was changed.
He was first enfeoffed Prince of Guangxing; later the state followed the commandery and the name was changed.
隨郡 is 'followed the commandery', not the toponym Suizhou.
Prince of Hedong, Xuan, styled Xuanyi, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
Prince of Hedong, Xuan, styled Xuanyin, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
字宣胤 is Xuanyin; 胤 is yin, not yi.
Prince of Hedong Xuan, styled Xuanyi, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
Prince of Hedong Xuan, styled Xuanyin, was the founding emperor's nineteenth son.
The literal courtesy name must also be Xuanyin for 宣胤.
When the High Emperor executed the princes, because Xuan was young and weak in talent he was not harmed.
When Gaozong executed the princes, because Xuan was young and weak in talent he was not harmed.
高宗 is the temple name Gaozong; High Emperor would render 高帝, a different person.
